implementation_notes: Rust has no code before main and no reflection, so the kit is explicit: a static OnceLock<HashMap<&str, fn() -> Box<dyn Shape>>> initialized once with get_or_init (stable since 1.70), builders as function pointers or boxed closures, and create(name) returning Option or Result instead of panicking. The table is a published snapshot - after the first initialisation it cannot change, which removes both the data race and the ordering hazard but also means tests want their own Registry value rather than the process-wide static. Function pointers capture nothing, so dependencies must arrive as arguments to create() or the builder must become Box<dyn Fn() -> Box<dyn Shape> + Send + Sync>; when registration must stay open at run time, swap OnceLock for RwLock and keep the table behind a guard.
pitfalls: OnceLock is initialised at most once, so this variant cannot unregister or add types after the first create; tests that need isolation must build a local table instead of touching the static.
fn pointers capture nothing: a builder needing configuration, a pool or a logger must be a boxed closure, which changes the table's type and adds Send + Sync bounds.
Errors are values here - returning Option silently loses the reason and returning Result forces every caller to handle it, so decide the missing-key policy once and apply it in create().

variants.name: Distributed registration collected at link time (inventory)
variants.implementation_notes: To avoid a central list of types, crates submit registration entries with inventory::submit! and the host iterates inventory::iter::<Registration>() - the linker collects the entries, so registration crosses crate boundaries without any runtime initialisation and still with no code before main. The price is a dependency on the crate and on link-section support, plus a silent failure mode: an entry is present only if the defining crate is linked and not dropped, so dead-code elimination or a missing reference can remove registrations without a compile error. Prefer the explicit OnceLock table when determinism and testability outweigh the decoupling; reach for inventory when plugin crates must not be enumerated by the host at all.
pitfalls: The mechanism rests on platform-specific link sections; on a target that does not support them the program still compiles but collects nothing.

Registration is invisible to reachability analysis: if the defining crate is linked but never referenced, the linker may drop the entry, so plugins need whole-archive-style linkage or a host-side reference.
There is no ordering and no duplicate detection - two crates may submit the same name, so the host must decide whether a collision is an error and check it at build time.
